newsitem.title: USA: Clinton bank reform plan due Monday delayed.
newsitem.headline: Clinton bank reform plan due Monday delayed.

text.p: The Clinton administration's plan to overhaul U.S. banking laws, expected to be released on Monday, will not be announced for several weeks, Treasury Department officials said.
"It looks like it will be mid to late April," one official said. "There are still a number of policy recommendations that haven't been narrowed down."

Congress is already hotly debating bank reform, with several bills introduced to tear down the Depression-era barriers separating banking from other financial services industries like insurance and securities underwriting.

Some of the plans would go even further and allow banks to combine with nonfinancial firms, like computer companies or department store chains. That approach has drawn fire from several quarters, including small banks, consumer groups and House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach.
Treasury officials have indicated that the administration favors tearing down the barriers between banking and other financial service industries.
Several months ago, the administration was also expected to endorse unlimited mixing of banking and commerce, but it was reconsidering that approach recently.
A Treasury official denied that the banking and commerce controversy alone was holding up the package. "It's not one specific thing," the official said.

Under a law enacted last year to shore up the savings industry's federal deposit insurance fund, the administration was directed to report to Congress by March 31 about the possibility of merging the operating charters of thrifts and banks.

Administration officials planned to use the report to outline their views on comprehensive bank reform. The report, now expected in a few weeks, could be in the form of a legislative proposal or a policy document, officials said.
